entries.title: Types
entries.summary: Primitive and built-in type forms used by Thrust.
entries.text:
Types
Primitive and built-in type forms used by Thrust.
Thrust types are written explicitly. Integers, floats, pointers, arrays, function references, and void all appear directly in source code.
This makes declarations easy to read. When a function takes u32, ptr[s32], or array[char; 64], the size and shape of the value are visible at the call boundary.
Use concrete types in public APIs unless there is a clear reason to introduce a type alias or a generic parameter.
Fixed-width integers are best for public APIs and binary formats because their size is part of the name.
Pointers and arrays mean different things. A pointer refers to memory elsewhere, while an array type describes a sequence of elements.
Prefer explicit widths like `u32` or `s64` when size matters.
Represent fixed-size protocol data with arrays, not dynamic buffers.
Use aliases when a plain type needs a clearer name.
var signed: s32 = -1;
var unsigned: u64 = 1;
var decimal: f64 = 3.14;
var bufferPtr: ptr[u8] = nullptr;
var dynamic: array[s32] = [1, 2, 3];
var fixedValues: array[u16; 4] = fixed[0, 1, 2, 3];
fn main() s32 @public {
    var values: array[s32; 3] = fixed[2, 4, 6];

    var sum: s32 =
        (deref values[0]) +
        (deref values[1]) +
        (deref values[2]);

    return sum;
}
Scalar Types
Scalar values are stored directly and are usually passed by value.
Signed integers use the s prefix, such as s8, s16, s32, and s64. Use them when negative values are part of the domain.
Unsigned integers use the u prefix, such as u8, u16, u32, and u64. Use them for sizes, bit masks, and values that cannot be negative.
Floating-point values use f32 or f64 in normal code. Wider or target-specific float forms should be kept near code that needs that representation.
bool represents true or false values. Keep boolean names descriptive because the type alone does not explain the condition.
char stores a byte-sized character value. Strings and UTF-8 data should still be treated as byte sequences unless a helper decodes code points.
Pointer and Array Types
Pointer and array syntax makes memory shape visible at the use site.
ptr[T] points to a value of type T. The pointer may still be null or invalid, so code must check the value before dereferencing when the source is not trusted.
ptr without a subtype is a raw pointer. Use it at FFI or allocator boundaries and cast back to a concrete pointer before reading typed values.
array[T] describes a dynamic array form. Its length is not part of the type.
array[T; N] describes a fixed-size array. The element count is part of the type and can be used by compile-time layout checks.
CString is the builtin alias used for null-terminated character arrays passed to C-style APIs.
Aliases and Layout
Aliases and layout builtins help keep public declarations readable without hiding representation.
type aliases give a name to an existing type. They do not create a separate runtime representation.
sizeOf, alignOf, and typeWidth report layout information known to the compiler. Use them for constants and static checks instead of repeating numeric assumptions.
ABI-oriented builtins such as abiSizeOf and abiAlignOf describe the representation required by the target ABI. Use them when interfacing with external code.

entries.title: Constants
entries.summary: Compile-time values that cannot be reassigned.
entries.text:
Constants
Compile-time values that cannot be reassigned.
Constants define values known at compile time. They are useful for sizes, flags, protocol values, and other numbers that should not be repeated throughout the code.
Constants can be built from compile-time helpers such as sizeOf and alignOf. That keeps layout-related values tied to the type they describe.
Use constants when the value is part of the program definition, not something that changes at runtime.
A constant cannot be reassigned. The compiler can use the value directly wherever the constant is referenced.
Keep constants near the code or module they describe. Very large global constant files are harder to maintain.
Define capacities once and reuse them across modules.
Use constants to derive array sizes and static checks.
Name constants after what they mean, not just after their type.
const U32_SIZE: usize = sizeOf(u32);
const F64_ALIGN: u32 = alignOf(f64);
const READY: bool = true;
const BUFFER_CAPACITY: usize = 1024;

fn capacity() usize @public {
    return BUFFER_CAPACITY;
}
Compile-Time Values
Constants are resolved while the program is compiled.
const name: Type = value declares a value that cannot be reassigned.
A constant expression can include literals and compile-time builtins such as sizeOf, alignOf, and pointerWidth.
Use constants for protocol values, flags, array sizes, ABI checks, and limits that are part of the program definition.
Constants Versus Variables
Use constants when the value is a rule, not state.
A variable stores runtime state and can change as the function executes.
A constant documents a fixed decision and lets the compiler reuse that value directly.
If a value depends on input, file contents, allocation, or an external call, it belongs in runtime code instead of a const declaration.

entries.title: Builtins
entries.summary: Compiler-provided functions, low-level memory and ABI operations, and builtin types for type, target, host, and compile-time work.
entries.text:
Builtins
Compiler-provided functions, low-level memory and ABI operations, and builtin types for type, target, host, and compile-time work.
Builtins are compiler-provided functions and reserved operations. Some return information about types, some return information about the target or host, and some help validate assumptions while compiling.
They are often used in constants and static checks. For example, sizeOf(u32) can define a constant, staticAssert can stop compilation if an assumption is wrong, and target builtins can select one branch over another before code generation.
Use builtins when the value belongs to the compiler, the ABI, the target machine, or low-level memory operations rather than to ordinary runtime program state.
Compile-time builtins are evaluated while the compiler processes the program, and memory and ABI builtins lower directly to low-level memory operations, ABI queries, or compiler-managed variadic argument access.
When staticAssert or compileError fails, compilation stops immediately. Warnings produced by compileWarning continue compilation but still affect diagnostics output.
Use staticAssert for layout and target assumptions.
Store builtin results in named constants when they are reused.
Prefer the highest-level builtin that states your intent clearly, then drop to memory and ABI builtins only when you really need raw memory behavior or ABI-level access.
Write staticAssert messages that clearly say what failed.
const SIZE: usize = sizeOf(u32);
const ALIGN: u32 = alignOf(u32);

fn verifyTypes() void {
    staticAssert(isSameType(u32, u32), "type mismatch");
}
const PTR_BITS: usize = pointerWidth();

fn verify() void @public {
    staticAssert(PTR_BITS == 64 or PTR_BITS == 32, "unsupported pointer width");
}
Type Layout Builtins
These builtins describe the size and layout of a type as the compiler sees it.
sizeOf(Type) - returns the size of a type in bytes as usize.
alignOf(Type) - returns the memory alignment of a type as u32.
typeWidth(Type) - returns the bit width of a type as usize.
fieldCount(Type) - returns the number of fields in a struct type as usize.
Type Information Builtins
These builtins answer structural questions about types.
fixedArraySize(Type) - returns the element count of a fixed-size array type as usize.
isSameType(A, B) - returns true when both types are exactly the same.
isPtrLike(Type) - returns true when the type is a pointer or another pointer-like type.
isFixedArrayOfSize(Type, N) - returns true when the type is a fixed array with exactly N elements.
Source Location Builtins
These builtins expose the source position currently being compiled.
file() - returns the current source file as a constant string.
fileLine() - returns the current source line as u32.
currentFuncName() - returns the current function name as a constant string.
Compile-Time Check Builtins
These builtins validate assumptions or emit diagnostics during compilation.
staticAssert(condition, "message") - stops compilation when the constant condition is false.
compileError("message") - always stops compilation with the given error message.
compileWarning("message") - emits a compile-time warning with the given message.
Compiler Information Builtins
These builtins report facts about the compiler itself.
compilerVersion() - returns the compiler version as a constant string.
debugBuild() - returns true when the compiler itself is a debug build.
String Builtins
These builtins operate on constant strings known to the compiler.
stringLength(string) - returns the length of a constant string as usize.
Type Predicate Builtins
These builtins return booleans about general type categories.
isSigned(Type) - returns true when the type is a signed integer type.
isUnsigned(Type) - returns true when the type is an unsigned integer type.
isInteger(Type) - returns true when the type is any integer type.
isFloat(Type) - returns true when the type is a floating-point type.
isBool(Type) - returns true when the type is bool.
isChar(Type) - returns true when the type is char.
isPointer(Type) - returns true when the type is a pointer.
isArray(Type) - returns true when the type is an array form.
isFixedArray(Type) - returns true when the type is a fixed-size array.
isStruct(Type) - returns true when the type is a struct type.
isVoid(Type) - returns true when the type is void.
isConst(Type) - returns true when the type has const qualification.
isNumeric(Type) - returns true when the type is numeric.
isFunction(Type) - returns true when the type is a function reference type.
Target Information Builtins
These builtins report what kind of machine and ABI the compiler is targeting.
targetOS() - returns the target operating system name as a constant string.
targetArch() - returns the target architecture name as a constant string.
targetVendor() - returns the target vendor name as a constant string.
targetAbi() - returns the target ABI name as a constant string.
targetTriple() - returns the full target triple as a constant string.
isLinux() - returns true when the target OS is Linux.
isWindows() - returns true when the target OS is Windows.
isDarwin() - returns true when the target OS is Darwin-based.
isApple() - returns true when the target vendor or platform is Apple-related.
isAix() - returns true when the target OS is AIX.
is64Bit() - returns true when the target pointer width is 64 bits.
is32Bit() - returns true when the target pointer width is 32 bits.
isBigEndian() - returns true when the target byte order is big-endian.
isLittleEndian() - returns true when the target byte order is little-endian.
isX86() - returns true when the target architecture is x86.
isX8664() - returns true when the target architecture is x86_64.
isArm() - returns true when the target architecture is ARM.
isAarch64() - returns true when the target architecture is AArch64.
isRiscv64() - returns true when the target architecture is RISC-V 64-bit.
isPpc() - returns true when the target architecture is PowerPC.
isPpc64() - returns true when the target architecture is PowerPC 64-bit.
isMips64() - returns true when the target architecture is MIPS64.
isSystemz() - returns true when the target architecture is IBM System z.
isLoongarch64() - returns true when the target architecture is LoongArch64.
isWasm() - returns true when the target architecture is WebAssembly.
isElf() - returns true when the target object format is ELF.
isMachO() - returns true when the target object format is Mach-O.
isCoff() - returns true when the target object format is COFF.
hasPosixThreads() - returns true when the target environment supports POSIX threads.
hasSysvAbi() - returns true when the target follows the System V ABI family.
pointerWidth() - returns the target ptr width in bits as usize.
isizeWidth() - returns the target ssize width in bits as usize.
usizeWidth() - returns the target usize width in bits as usize.
pointerAlign() - returns the pointer alignment in bytes as usize.
maxAlignment() - returns the maximum supported alignment in bytes as usize.
targetCPU() - returns the target CPU name as a constant string.
targetCpuFeatures() - returns the enabled target CPU features as a constant string.
hasFeature("name") - returns true when the target CPU supports the named feature.
Host Information Builtins
These builtins report facts about the machine running the compiler, not the machine being targeted.
hostOsName() - returns the host operating system name as a constant string.
hostArch() - returns the host architecture name as a constant string.
hostEndian() - returns the host endianness as a constant string.
currentTimestamp() - returns the current host timestamp as usize.
Memory and ABI Builtins
These builtins lower directly to low-level memory operations, ABI queries, or variadic argument access.
halloc(Type) - allocates heap memory for one value of the given type and returns ptr[Type].
memcpy(dst, src, size) - copies a block of memory and returns ptr.
memmove(dst, src, size) - moves a block of memory safely for overlapping ranges and returns ptr.
memset(dst, value, size) - fills a memory block with a byte value and returns ptr.
abiSizeOf(Type) - returns the ABI-defined size of a type in bytes as u64.
bitSizeOf(Type) - returns the size of a type in bits as u64.
abiAlignOf(Type) - returns the ABI-defined alignment of a type as u32.
arbitraryArgs() - returns the current variadic argument list as ptr.
arbitraryArg(Type) - reads one variadic argument of the given type.
Builtin Type
The language also exposes one builtin alias that appears in many APIs.
CString - builtin alias for array[char], used for null-terminated string values.
Using Builtins in Declarations
Builtins are most useful when they keep declarations tied to target facts.
Use sizeOf and alignOf to define capacities or layout checks that follow the referenced type.
Use target builtins to select platform-specific constants and imports through compile-time conditionals.
Use compileError and compileWarning for explicit diagnostics when a configuration is unsupported or unusual.

entries.title: Compiler Command Line Reference
entries.summary: Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
This section explains the command line flags available in Thrust Compiler v0.2.0 and gives a practical view of what each group of options is for.
Use it when you need a stable reference for compilation, linking, diagnostics, emitted outputs, or target selection in this archived release.
Each category groups related flags together and includes accepted values, examples, and notes based on the published v0.2.0 command line snapshot.
thrustc main.thrust -opt O2 -emit llvm-ir
thrustc main.thrust -target-triple x86_64-pc-linux-gnu -abi system-v
thrustc main.thrust --help emit

entries.title: General Commands
entries.summary: Entry-point commands for help, version, and diagnostic explanations.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
General Commands
Entry-point commands for help, version, and diagnostic explanations.
These commands do not primarily configure code generation. They are used to inspect the compiler, request help, or explain diagnostics.
-h
--help
optional help topic
opt
emit
print
code-model
reloc-model
sanitizer
symbol-linkage-strategy
denormal-floating-point-behavior
denormal-floating-point-32-bits-behavior
Show the compiler help message.
Without an extra topic, this prints the full top-level command line help.
With a supported topic, it prints the focused help for that flag family instead of the generic overview.
thrustc --help
thrustc --help emit
Topics are optional. Unsupported topics fall back to the general help output.
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-v
--version
Print the compiler version and exit.
This does not start a compilation pipeline. It only prints the current compiler version string.
thrustc --version
--explain
diagnostic code
E0001
W0001
Show the explanation for a compiler error or warning code.
Use this when you already have a diagnostic code and want the longer explanation text.
The accepted value is a compiler issue code such as an error or warning identifier.
thrustc --explain E0001
The exact available codes depend on the compiler version.
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.

entries.title: Linkage Flags
entries.summary: Flags that select or configure the external linker toolchain.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
Linkage Flags
Flags that select or configure the external linker toolchain.
These flags control which external C or C++ compiler participates in the linking stage and what raw arguments it receives.
-link-with-clang
path/to/clang
Specify the external Clang binary used for the linking stage.
This forces the linker driver to use a specific Clang executable instead of automatic detection.
It is useful when more than one LLVM or Clang toolchain is installed on the machine.
thrustc main.thrust -link-with-clang /usr/bin/clang
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-link-with-gcc
path/to/gcc
Specify the external GCC binary used for the linking stage.
This selects GCC as the external linking compiler.
Use it when you want GCC-specific linking behavior or when GCC is the available host linker toolchain.
thrustc main.thrust -link-with-gcc /usr/bin/gcc
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cc-args
"-lm;-lz"
Forward raw arguments to the active external C or C++ linking compiler.
This is the escape hatch for linker or C compiler options that do not have a first-class Thrust flag.
Arguments can be separated by spaces or semicolons inside the raw string.
thrustc main.thrust -cc-args "-lm;-lz"
This value is treated as a raw argument list and is split by the CLI preprocessor.
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.

entries.title: Compiler Flags
entries.summary: Core compilation, backend, target, JIT, ABI, and debug flags.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
Compiler Flags
Core compilation, backend, target, JIT, ABI, and debug flags.
These flags shape the actual compilation pipeline: targets, outputs, optimization, JIT execution, standard library resolution, ABI behavior, and debug information.
-build-dir
path/to/build
Set the directory used for generated compiler artifacts.
Use this when you want emitted files, intermediates, and temporary build outputs to live outside the default location.
thrustc main.thrust -build-dir build/
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-tools-dir
path/to/tools
Set the compiler tools directory used to find external helper tools.
This points the compiler at a tools root that expands what it can discover automatically during the pipeline.
thrustc main.thrust -tools-dir ./tools
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-target
architecture name
x86_64
Set the target architecture.
Use this when the desired architecture is enough and you do not need to spell a full target triple.
thrustc main.thrust -target x86_64
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-target-triple
target triple
x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
Set the full target triple used for code generation and linking decisions.
The target triple controls operating system, architecture, vendor, and ABI assumptions in one place.
Prefer this over `-target` when cross-compiling or when the platform details matter.
thrustc main.thrust -target-triple x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cpu
cpu name
haswell
alderlake
ivybridge
pentium
pantherlake
Select the CPU model used for optimization and code generation tuning.
This helps the backend emit code for a specific processor family rather than a generic architecture.
thrustc main.thrust -cpu haswell
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cpu-enable-features
feature;feature
sse2
cx16
sahf
tbm
Enable specific CPU features in addition to the CPU baseline.
Use this when you want to turn on a small set of backend features without replacing the whole feature list.
thrustc main.thrust -cpu-enable-features sse2;cx16
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cpu-disable-features
feature;feature
sse2
cx16
sahf
tbm
Disable specific CPU features from the active configuration.
This is useful when the selected CPU baseline is too aggressive for the actual deployment environment.
thrustc main.thrust -cpu-disable-features tbm
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cpu-features
+feature,-feature
+sse2
+cx16
+sahf
-tbm
Replace the CPU feature set with an explicit signed list.
This gives direct low-level control over the backend feature string.
Use it when you want an explicit allow and deny list rather than incremental enable or disable flags.
thrustc main.thrust -cpu-features +sse2,+cx16,-tbm
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-emit
artifact kind
llvm-bc
llvm-ir
asm
unopt-llvm-ir
unopt-llvm-bc
unopt-asm
obj
unchecked-pretty-ast
unchecked-ast
pretty-ast
ast
pretty-tokens
tokens
Emit one selected compilation artifact instead of performing only the default end-to-end flow.
Use emission when you want a file output such as LLVM IR, assembler, object code, tokens, or AST snapshots.
thrustc main.thrust -emit llvm-ir
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-print
printable unit
llvm-ir
unopt-llvm-ir
asm
unopt-asm
unchecked-pretty-ast
unchecked-ast
pretty-ast
ast
pretty-tokens
tokens
Print one selected compilation representation to standard output.
This is the text-output twin of `-emit`.
Use it for inspection, debugging, or piping compiler output into another tool.
thrustc main.thrust -print tokens
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-opt
optimization level
O0
O1
O2
O3
Os
Oz
Choose the optimization level.
Higher levels generally trade compilation time for more aggressive optimization.
Use size-oriented levels when output size matters more than raw performance.
thrustc main.thrust -opt O2
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-stop-at
pipeline stage
lexing
parsing
scope-analysis
ast-verification
type-checking
general-analysis
attribute-checking
linter
compiler-intrinsic-checking
compiler-callconventions-checking
codegen
Stop the pipeline after a selected compiler stage.
This is useful for debugging the compiler pipeline and inspecting partial outputs.
thrustc main.thrust -stop-at parsing
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-reloc-model
relocation model
static
pic
dynamic
Select how the backend handles relocations and external symbol references.
This affects generated machine code and the way addresses are represented.
Use PIC-related modes when the output must be position independent.
thrustc main.thrust -reloc-model pic
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-code-model
code model
small
medium
large
kernel
Choose the backend code model.
The code model influences assumptions about code and data placement in the address space.
thrustc main.thrust -code-model small
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-macos-version
version
15.0.0
Set the macOS SDK or deployment version used for Apple targets.
Use this when you need the generated output to match a specific macOS deployment baseline.
thrustc main.thrust -macos-version 15.0.0
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-ios-version
version
17.4.0
Set the iOS SDK or deployment version used for Apple mobile targets.
This matters when targeting Apple mobile environments and their deployment constraints.
thrustc main.thrust -ios-version 17.4.0
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-cuda-version
version
2.0
Set the NVIDIA CUDA version used for CUDA-oriented compilation flows.
This lets the compiler adapt CUDA-related ABI or backend expectations for a particular CUDA release.
thrustc kernel.thrust -cuda-version 2.0
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-jit
Enable the JIT execution mode.
With JIT enabled, the compiler prepares the program for in-process execution instead of only generating files.
thrustc main.thrust -jit
Some other JIT flags only make sense when this flag is already active.
-jit-libc
path/to/libc.so
Set the C runtime used by the JIT execution flow.
Use this when the JIT runtime must link against a specific C runtime library.
thrustc main.thrust -jit -jit-libc /usr/lib/libc.so
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-jit-link
path/to/library.so
Add an extra shared library for JIT execution.
This lets the JIT loader resolve external symbols from additional libraries.
thrustc main.thrust -jit -jit-link /usr/lib/libraylib.so
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-jit-entry
symbol name
Set the entry point symbol used by JIT execution.
Use this when the executed function is not the default `main`.
thrustc main.thrust -jit -jit-entry run
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-jit-args
"--foo;bar"
Pass arguments to the program executed through the JIT runtime.
Arguments are passed through the JIT configuration rather than through the host shell after compilation.
thrustc main.thrust -jit -jit-args "--name;demo"
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-abi
ABI name
system-v
nvidia-cuda
Select the ABI used for code generation.
The ABI affects calling conventions, data passing rules, and interoperability with external code.
thrustc main.thrust -abi system-v
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-mode
feature mode
stable
unstable
Select the compiler features mode.
Stable mode limits the language surface to stable features.
Unstable mode enables experimental or incomplete features.
thrustc main.thrust -mode stable
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-std
path/to/std
Set the standard library root path.
Use this when the compiler should resolve the standard library from a non-default location.
thrustc main.thrust -std ./std
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-std-version
x.x.x
Set the standard library version to use.
This helps the compiler resolve the expected versioned standard library snapshot.
thrustc main.thrust -std-version 0.2.0
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
-dbg
Enable generation of debug information.
This turns on backend debug info emission such as DWARF data where supported.
thrustc main.thrust -dbg
-dbg-for-inlining
Emit debug information optimized for inlined functions.
Use this when debugging optimized builds where inlining would otherwise hide useful location information.
thrustc main.thrust -dbg -dbg-for-inlining
-dbg-for-profiling
Emit extra debug information for source-level profiling tools.
This helps profilers map optimized machine code back to the original source more accurately.
thrustc main.thrust -dbg-for-profiling
-dbg-dwarf-version
DWARF version
v4
v5
Set the DWARF version used for debug information.
Use this when your debugger or platform requires a specific DWARF generation.
thrustc main.thrust -dbg-dwarf-version v5
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--disable-abi
Disable ABI detection and ABI-specific code generation behavior.
This can be useful for debugging or for niche targets where automatic ABI handling gets in the way.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-abi
--denormal-floating-point-behavior
mode list
IEEE
preserve-sign-signature
transform-to-positive-zero
dynamic
Control how denormal floating-point values are handled for general floating-point operations.
This affects how the backend treats denormal values and therefore can change numerical edge-case behavior.
thrustc main.thrust --denormal-floating-point-behavior IEEE
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--denormal-floating-point-32-bits-behavior
mode list
IEEE
preserve-sign-signature
transform-to-positive-zero
dynamic
Control how denormal 32-bit floating-point values are handled.
This is the 32-bit specific counterpart of the general denormal floating-point behavior flag.
thrustc main.thrust --denormal-floating-point-32-bits-behavior IEEE
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--symbol-linkage-strategy
strategy
any
exact
large
samesize
noduplicates
Choose the strategy used when symbol linkages need to be merged or reconciled.
This matters when the backend has to reason about multiple declarations of the same symbol.
thrustc main.thrust --symbol-linkage-strategy exact
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--stack-protector
Enable stack protection instrumentation.
This inserts stack state protection intended to make some classes of memory corruption harder to exploit.
thrustc main.thrust --stack-protector
--sanitizer
sanitizer
address
hwaddress
memory
thread
memtag
Enable one selected sanitizer runtime and its instrumentation.
Sanitizers add runtime checks and diagnostics for memory issues, threading bugs, or related classes of problems.
thrustc main.thrust --sanitizer address
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--no-sanitize
setting;setting
bounds
coverage
Disable specific sanitizer subfeatures or code emission details.
Use this to narrow or tune the effect of an active sanitizer configuration.
thrustc main.thrust --sanitizer address --no-sanitize bounds
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--opt-passes
-p{passname,passname}
Pass a custom LLVM optimization pass list.
Use this when the default optimization pipeline is not enough and you want to control LLVM pass selection directly.
thrustc main.thrust --opt-passes -p{instcombine,sroa}
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--modificator-passes
pass;pass
loopvectorization

loopinterleaving
loopsimplifyvectorization
mergefunctions
callgraphprofile
Pass a custom modificator optimization pass list.
This lets you tune the pass set used by the compiler-specific modificator stage.
thrustc main.thrust --modificator-passes loopvectorization;loopunroll
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--target-triple-darwin-variant
variant triple
arm64-apple-ios15.0-macabi
Set the Darwin target variant triple.
Use this when a Darwin target needs its variant triple spelled out separately from the main target triple.
thrustc main.thrust --target-triple-darwin-variant arm64-apple-ios15.0-macabi
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--enable-ansi-color
Enable ANSI color formatting in diagnostics output.
This is useful when the compiler runs in terminals or logs that preserve ANSI escape sequences.
thrustc main.thrust --enable-ansi-color

entries.title: Disable Compiler Flags
entries.summary: Flags that switch off selected backend, math, sanitizer, or optimization behaviors.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
Disable Compiler Flags
Flags that switch off selected backend, math, sanitizer, or optimization behaviors.
These flags turn off optional behavior that would otherwise be active, either by default or because of another active mode.
--disable-frame-pointer
Omit frame pointer emission regardless of optimization level.
This can reduce overhead or follow platform-specific conventions, but it can also make debugging and stack walking harder.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-frame-pointer
--disable-uwtable
Omit unwind table emission.
This can reduce output size, but it may hurt exception handling support or stack tracing quality.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-uwtable
--disable-direct-access-external-data
Force external data references to be accessed indirectly instead of directly.
This changes how the backend reaches external data symbols and can matter for relocation or platform constraints.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-direct-access-external-data
--disable-rtlib-got
Disable the runtime library dependency on the Global Offset Table.
The original help text describes this as useful for some ARM non-PIC situations.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-rtlib-got
--disable-safe-trapping-math
Allow trapping math operations instead of forcing safer behavior.
This mainly affects floating-point code paths where the backend would otherwise avoid trap-prone behavior.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-safe-trapping-math
--disable-safe-math
Disable safe integer math behavior.
This allows overflow-oriented or less constrained math behavior at the cost of stronger guarantees.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-safe-math
--disable-default-optimization
Disable the default optimization work that would otherwise happen even without an explicit optimization flag.
This is the spelling shown in the local v0.2.0 release snapshot.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-default-optimization
--disable-all-sanitizers
Disable all sanitizers.
Use this to clear sanitizer instrumentation globally for the current compilation.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-all-sanitizers
--disable-all-cpu-features
Disable all CPU feature toggles.
This clears CPU feature assumptions back toward a minimal baseline.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-all-cpu-features

entries.title: Warning Compiler Flags
entries.summary: Flags that suppress warning diagnostics.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
Warning Compiler Flags
Flags that suppress warning diagnostics.
These flags affect how warning diagnostics are emitted and filtered.
--disable-warnings
W0001;W0005;W0010
Disable selected warning codes.
Use this when a known warning is intentionally triggered and you want to silence it locally for the current build.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-warnings W0001;W0005
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--disable-all-warnings
Disable all general and specific warnings.
This suppresses warning diagnostics broadly and should be used carefully.
thrustc main.thrust --disable-all-warnings

entries.title: Other Compiler Flags
entries.summary: Quality-of-life, cleanup, diagnostic export, and discovery flags.
entries.text:
Compiler Command Line Reference
Detailed reference for the Thrust compiler command line flags in v0.2.0.
Other Compiler Flags
Quality-of-life, cleanup, diagnostic export, and discovery flags.
These flags do not fit the core target or codegen categories. They mostly help with inspection, cleanup, exports, and tool discovery.
--copy-output-to-clipboard
Copy the printable compiler output to the system clipboard.
This only makes sense when a `-print` flag is also active and the platform clipboard integration is available.
thrustc main.thrust -print ast --copy-output-to-clipboard
--debug-clang-command
Display the generated Clang command used during linking.
This helps inspect or debug the external command the compiler is about to run.
thrustc main.thrust --debug-clang-command
--debug-gcc-command
Display the generated GCC command used during linking.
This is the GCC counterpart of `--debug-clang-command`.
thrustc main.thrust --debug-gcc-command
--export-compiler-errors
Export compiler error diagnostics to files.
Use this when you want diagnostics persisted instead of only printed to the terminal.
thrustc main.thrust --export-compiler-errors
--export-compiler-warnings
Export compiler warning diagnostics to files.
This is useful for build automation or post-processing warning results.
thrustc main.thrust --export-compiler-warnings
--export-diagnostics-path
diagnostics/
Set the directory used for exported diagnostics.
Use this with diagnostic export flags to control where the compiler writes its files.
thrustc main.thrust --export-compiler-errors --export-diagnostics-path diagnostics/
This flag accepts a value separated by a space, `=` or `:`.
--clean-exported-diagnostics
Clean the exported diagnostics directory.
This removes or resets previously exported diagnostic files before or after a compilation workflow.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-exported-diagnostics
--clean-build
Clean the compiler build directory.
Use this to remove accumulated compilation artifacts.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-build
--clean-tokens
Clean the directory that stores lexical token outputs.
This is mostly useful when using token emission or token printing workflows.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-tokens
--clean-assembler
Clean the directory that stores emitted assembler files.
This helps keep emitted assembler output tidy between builds.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-assembler
--clean-llvm-ir
Clean the directory that stores emitted LLVM IR files.
Use this when repeatedly emitting IR and you want a clean output directory.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-llvm-ir
--clean-llvm-bitcode
Clean the directory that stores emitted LLVM bitcode files.
This is the bitcode-specific cleanup flag.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-llvm-bitcode
--clean-objects
Clean the directory that stores emitted object files.
Use this when object file output should be reset before a new build.
thrustc main.thrust --clean-objects
--dump-compiler-version
Write the compiler version into `COMPILER_VERSION.txt`.
This exports the version string to a flat text file in the working directory.
thrustc --dump-compiler-version
--no-obfuscate-archive-names
Disable file-name obfuscation for archive names.
The original help text notes that this does not apply to the final build output.
thrustc main.thrust --no-obfuscate-archive-names
--no-obfuscate-ir
Disable name obfuscation in emitted IR output.
This is useful when emitted IR should stay easier to read or diff.
thrustc main.thrust -emit llvm-ir --no-obfuscate-ir
--print-targets
Print the supported targets.
Use this to inspect which targets are currently known by the compiler build.
thrustc --print-targets
--print-supported-cpus
Print the supported CPUs for the current target.
This helps choose a valid value for `-cpu`.
thrustc --print-supported-cpus
--print-host-target-triple
Print the host target triple.
This reports the native triple of the machine running the compiler.
thrustc --print-host-target-triple
--print-opt-passes
Print the optimization passes available through `--opt-passes`.
This is a discovery flag for users who want to build a custom pass list.
thrustc --print-opt-passes
